newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Fighting, explosions overshadow Abkhaz vote.
newsitem.headline: Fighting, explosions overshadow Abkhaz vote.

text.p: Sporadic fighting and a series of explosions on Saturday overshadowed the parliamentary election in Georgia's breakaway region of Abkhazia, denounced by Tbilisi, Moscow and the West.

An Abkhaz Interior Ministry official said Georgian partisans armed with grenade launchers and automatic weapons launched cross-border attacks in the east of Abkhazia, the only part of the region still predominantly populated by ethnic Georgians.
He said one Abkhaz policeman had been injured in a two-pronged attack in a border village.

The official said time-controlled mines had gone off in at least three polling stations in the Gali area, to the south-east of the regional capital Sukhumi and close to the border with government-controlled Georgia.
Reporters visiting the town in the morning heard sporadic explosions and saw two damaged polling stations.
The Georgian government says Saturday's vote called by the self-styled Abkhaz government of Vladislav Ardzinba is illegal but has denied any links with the alleged "sabotage units".
Mostly elderly ethnic Georgians were voting in Gali. While they said they were doing so voluntarily, some townspeople said residents were afraid of Abkhaz retribution if they did not cast ballots.

About 10 armed Abkhazians guarded one polling station and voters were handed ballots with a single candidate listed. There was no voting booth and an election official sat directly behind the ballot box.

"They are afraid the Georgians will punish them if they do vote and afraid the Abkhaz will if they don't. Since they are here in Abkhazia, they have to be more afraid of the Abkhaz," said a local woman selling cheese pies in a street cafe.
Blue-helmeted Russian peacekeepers cruised the streets in armoured vehicles and Abkhaz fighters combed the town for mines, formerly home to 60,000 people.
The United Nations observer mission in Gali appeared to have at least temporarily abandoned it's headquarters. U.N officals have said they feared trouble if the elections go forward.
Away from the Gali region, voting was proceeding calmly.
A steady stream of people began arriving at one central polling place in Sukhumi just after polls opened at 7 a.m. (0400GMT).
A long hall was decked out in green, red and white Abkhaz flags and portraits of separatist fighters killed in the bitter 1992-93 conflict with Georgian troops.

Abkhazia, a Black Sea coastal region once favoured by the Soviet communist elite, has run itself as an independent state since 1993 when its fighters routed Georgian government troops after a year-long war which cost 10,000 lives.
At least 150,000 ethnic Georgian refugees have still not returned to Abkhazia after they fled the conflict.
Georgia wants them to be allowed to return home and for political issues to be resolved before any elections.
The refugees take part in a parallel plebiscite organised by Tbilisi on Saturday in which they will get a chance to condemn the vote, going on without them, as illegitimate.
The U.N., the European Union and the Georgian government have called for the cancellation of the Abkhaz election, in which 81 candidates are vying for 35 parliamentary seats.

Russian officers still stationed in Abkhazia say openly that they were ordered to help the Abkhaz during the war with training, vast amounts of weapons and ammunition at a time when Georgia's relations with Moscow were bad.

But with Georgia now a member of the Commonwealth of Independent States, successor to the Soviet Union, and Russia facing separatist problems of its own, Moscow has told Abkhazia to forget independence and work out an arrangement with Tbilisi.
